countries.system_notes: Westminster parliamentary sovereignty. A government with a Commons majority can create a nationwide cash benefit by ordinary statute, and courts cannot strike down primary legislation. The Lords can delay money bills only 1 month and other public bills about 1 year under the Parliament Acts. Under the Salisbury convention the Lords do not block manifesto bills (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_Acts_1911_and_1949). There is no filibuster and no separately elected executive, so there are fewer veto points than in the US. Social security is essentially reserved to Westminster; delivery would run through HMRC/DWP and the existing Universal Credit system. Scotland cannot legislate a UBI alone: its own MIG roadmap needs further powers or UK cooperation (https://www.gov.scot/publications/minimum-income-guarantee-executive-summary/). The binding constraint is fiscal and market-based, not procedural. Debt was about 94.1% of GDP; 10-year gilts yielded about 5.27% and 30-year about 5.92%; headroom fell from £23.6bn to about £13bn by September 2026 (techtimes link above). Bond markets reacted even to Burnham's talk of 'flexibility'. The election can be called early; the latest date is 15 August 2029.

p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: Defined as a Labour single-party majority after the 2029 election (US D-trifecta analog). Manifold puts a Labour PM at 41.3%, but that includes minority and coalition outcomes. Polls are a near-tie: YouGov 27-28 Sep has Reform 25 / Lab 24, with Reform up 4 in a week; Opinium 9 Sep has Lab 27 / Ref 25. Five parties at 11% or more make a hung parliament likely, and the post-July 'Burnham bounce' is already eroding. If the dashboard counts any Labour-led government (including minority or coalition with LD/Greens) as left-led, use about 0.28/0.40/0.52 instead.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: A Reform or Conservative single-party majority. Manifold gives a Reform PM 32% and a Conservative PM 16.4%, but much of that mass sits in hung or coalition scenarios. 'Farage party wins' is 30.1%. Reform leads the latest YouGov (25%), and Con (19%) plus Reform together outpoll Labour, but the split right vote under FPTP limits majorities. Treat a Reform–Con coalition as right-like; including it moves this to about 0.45. The implied residual 'other' (hung parliament) is about 0.5.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: UK politics usually swings between Labour and Conservative majorities, but the current five-party fragmentation (every party at 11% or more in YouGov) raises hung-parliament odds for the 2030s too. After a Burnham term, alternation risk favors the right in 2029, then a partial reversion toward Labour. No long-horizon market exists.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Reform's local-election and polling strength and the possibility of right-bloc consolidation (Manifold prices a Reform–Con merger at only 5.2%) keep single-party right majorities plausible, but a split right vote caps them. The residual is about 0.37 'other'.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Comparable to a US D trifecta without a shock (0.01-0.07). This is pushed slightly up by Burnham's personal UBI sympathy and a 166-seat majority with no filibuster; a minister floated UBI for AI in January 2026. It is pushed down by Burnham's commitment to the Reeves fiscal rules, only £13bn of headroom, gilt stress (10y ~5.3%), Labour's preference for targeted UC plus universal services, and 56% of the public calling UBI unaffordable. A Greater Manchester or national pilot is far likelier than a qualifying statute.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: Both Reform (£50bn welfare cut, scrap PIP) and the Conservatives (30% UC cut, restricted benefit card) are campaigning on shrinking cash welfare. Only 31% of Reform voters and 21% of Conservative voters backed UBI in YouGov 2024.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta-in-shock mode (0.45) despite fewer veto points (Commons majority; Lords can only delay). There are three reasons. (1) The UK already has a national means-tested Universal Credit system (£424.90/month for a single adult 25+), so the path of least resistance in a 3pp unemployment shock is a UC uplift, which does not qualify. (2) Bond-market discipline is acute: yields hit multi-decade highs in 2026 and the Truss-style constraint binds. (3) Affordability skepticism is high. Pushing up: Burnham and parts of the cabinet have publicly entertained UBI for AI displacement, Green pressure on Labour's left flank is rising, and Labour voters back UBI 61%.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: A populist Reform government could conceivably pay a citizens-only 'dividend'; its platform already restricts benefits to citizens, and the qualifying definition only requires adult citizens. But its stated program is welfare retrenchment and work conditionality, and the Conservatives say 'if you can work, you should work'. Comparable to the US divided-government shock band (0.03-0.15), at the low end.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: A hung parliament mixes very different coalitions. Labour + LD + Green deals put UBI on the table (the Greens are committed; LDs prefer an income-tested GBI, which would be the likely compromise and would not qualify). Reform–Con arrangements are hostile. Coalition bargaining in a shock tends to produce UC top-ups.

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: The IMF (Gen-AI SDN 2024) finds about 60% of advanced-economy jobs AI-exposed and calibrates its model to the UK as 'highly exposed'. The UK has a large professional and financial services share. The labour market is already soft (ONS unemployment 4.9% in May-Jul 2026; weak graduate hiring). Downside: slower enterprise adoption than the US (lower per-capita Claude usage than the US and Canada per the Anthropic Economic Index), and a shock may be attributed to energy or gilt-driven austerity rather than AI.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Adoption trails the US modestly (Anthropic usage-index snippet: US 3.62, Canada 2.91, UK 2.67), and UK firms face more employment-protection friction, but UK services exposure is high. The IMF notes UK entry-level 'stepping-stone' jobs are vulnerable. A lag of about 1 year is the central case; the UK could be contemporaneous if London finance and professional services adopt quickly.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: UK GDP per capita is about US$54k (IMF 2026), roughly £45k (derived from £2.985tn debt = 94.1% of GDP over about 69-70m people). The UC single 25+ standard allowance (about £5.1k/yr) is about 11% of GDP per capita. A partial UBI of the Green 2015-scheme type (£80/week, about £4.2k/yr) is about 9%. The Wales pilot's £19.2k/yr (about 40%+) was a targeted pilot and is not scalable. A tax-neutral partial UBI replacing personal allowances would cluster at 6-10%.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: In a shock, a payment near or above the UC single-adult floor (about 11%) becomes the political anchor, since the Greens and the Labour left frame UBI as covering basic needs; half of UK UBI supporters want full living costs covered. Gilt-market limits cap the upper tail.

key_risks: Fiscal and bond-market constraint: debt about 94% of GDP, 10y gilts about 5.3% and 30y about 5.9% (2026 highs), headroom cut to about £13bn before the 28 Oct 2026 budget. Burnham has pledged to keep the fiscal rules, and even 'flexibility' talk moved yields.
Channel substitution: the mature, means-tested Universal Credit system makes a UC uplift the default shock response, which is non-qualifying. The Lib Dems' 'Guaranteed Basic Income' is also UC-based.
Right-bloc surge: Reform leads the latest YouGov (25%). Reform and the Conservatives both run on welfare cuts (£50bn; 30% UC cuts), which could lock in retrenchment for the 2029-34 term.

Leadership volatility: Burnham is Labour's second PM since 2024 after record local-election losses. A further leadership change or early election (Polymarket: 23% called by mid-2027) could remove the most UBI-sympathetic PM in UK history.
Public affordability skepticism: 56% say UBI is unaffordable, and support drops sharply when tax rises are specified (Bath/Ipsos: 49% to 30%).
Labour ideology favors universal basic services (National Care Service, public ownership) over universal cash.
Upside risk: a PM with a public pro-UBI record, a minister already linking AI to UBI, a 166-seat majority and a weak Lords make a fast enactment mechanically easy if a shock arrives during 2026-29.

countries.head_of_government: Mark Carney (Liberal), Prime Minister since 2025. He won the 2025 Liberal leadership after Trudeau resigned and led the Liberals to a minority in the April 2025 election. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/46th_Canadian_federal_election, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Mark_Carney
countries.governing_parties_and_majority: Liberal majority government, won mid-term. Three by-election wins on 13 April 2026 plus five floor-crossers since December 2025 (four ex-Conservative, one ex-NDP) took the Liberals to 174 seats against a 172-seat majority threshold (https://globalnews.ca/news/11798684/federal-byelections-2026/). Wikipedia currently lists Lib 173, Con 137, Bloc 21, NDP 5, Green 1, plus vacancies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/46th_Canadian_federal_election). This is a two-seat cushion. The opposition is Pierre Poilievre's Conservatives; the NDP (leader Avi Lewis since March 2026) is reduced to 5 seats.
countries.system_notes: Westminster system with a fixed-date election law that the PM can override by requesting a dissolution. A government bill with a Commons majority passes. The appointed Senate can reject bills but seldom does. Current Senate: ISG 40, CSG 18, PSG 17, Conservative 12, non-affiliated 8, 10 vacant. Money bills must originate in the Commons (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Canada). Federalism matters: provinces run social assistance, and the Bloc and Conservatives opposed C-223 partly on provincial-jurisdiction grounds (https://openparliament.ca/bills/44-1/C-223/). Ottawa can still pay individuals directly through CRA refundable credits: the CCB, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, the quarterly Canada Carbon Rebate until April 2025, and OAS. So a federal UBI could be delivered as a refundable credit to all adult tax-filers without provincial consent, though Quebec friction is likely. Private members' and Senate public bills rarely become law: S-206 is only a framework bill and would not itself create a payment. The live Canadian proposal (PBO costing, S-206) is an income-tested GBI with a 50% reduction rate, which would not qualify as UBI under this definition.

countries.left_bloc: The Liberal Party is the more UBI-receptive of the two parties that can form government. Its grassroots have repeatedly passed basic-income resolutions: in 2020 the caucus made a guaranteed basic income its top priority, and the 2023 convention's resolution #7 was 'Installing Guaranteed Liveable Basic Income'. But the Liberal government and most Liberal MPs voted down C-223 (54-273, 25 Sep 2024), and none of the 24 official 2026 convention resolutions concern basic income. The NDP and Greens are the committed GLBI parties but hold 6 seats together. For the model, 'left-led' means a Liberal single-party majority. A Liberal minority dependent on the NDP (like the 2022-24 supply-and-confidence deal) falls in 'other' but is slightly more receptive than a Liberal majority.

'Right-led' means a Conservative majority. The Bloc (21 seats) opposes federal basic income on jurisdictional grounds.

Roughly: P(Liberal most seats) ≈ 0.55 × P(majority | win) ≈ 0.6. If the dashboard counts any Liberal-led government as left-led, use about 0.42/0.55/0.68.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: A Conservative single-party majority. Kalshi has CPC at 42% to win, but the CPC is at 29-33% in September 2026 polls, Poilievre's leadership is contested (Manifold: 17% he is out by year-end), and floor-crossings have weakened the caucus. Implied residual 'other' (minority parliaments) is about 0.45.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Base rate: minority parliaments are common in Canada (2019, 2021, 2025), and after about 14+ years of Liberal government by 2029, alternation favors the Conservatives in the 2030s. Liberal majorities remain plausible given Conservative weakness in Quebec and BC.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Alternation pressure after a long Liberal run raises Conservative majority odds in 2033+. The residual is about 0.43 minority.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta normal band (mode 0.03). Liberals voted down C-223 in 2024 and dropped basic income from their 2026 convention resolutions. Carney's agenda is AI investment and retraining plus an income-tested affordability top-up (CGEB +25%). Critically, even a Liberal 'basic income' would most likely follow the PBO/S-206 income-tested GBI design (50% reduction rate), which fails the qualifying definition. Public support favors GBI (60/22) over UBI (37/42).

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: Conservatives oppose UBI on cost and work-incentive grounds and opposed C-223. The Bloc, a potential minority partner, rejects federal social programs in provincial jurisdiction.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: Lower than the US D-trifecta shock mode (0.45) despite fewer veto points (Commons majority, compliant Senate that already hosts a GLBI bill, CRA delivery channel proven by the CCB and Carbon Rebate). Canada's policy consensus and public opinion strongly favor income-testing, so a shock most likely yields an income-tested GBI or CERB-style temporary payment, which does not qualify. The Liberals are centrist rather than left. Pushing up: Carney has linked AI displacement to 'social supports', Liberal grassroots have backed GLBI for years, and the PBO shows a GBI can be near cost-neutral.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: A Conservative government in a 3pp AI shock would likely use EI extensions and targeted credits. Some conservative voices sympathize with basic income, but party policy opposes UBI. At the low end of the US divided-government shock band.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: Minority parliaments: a Liberal minority dependent on the NDP (pro-GLBI; the 2022-24 supply deal produced dental care and pharmacare) could pass a GLBI framework or an income-tested GBI, but universality is still the obstacle. cross_country.notes: Both countries are Westminster systems. A single-party Commons majority can pass a national cash benefit with fewer veto points than the US: no filibuster, and the Lords or Senate rarely block. That raises conditional enactment odds relative to the US. Two structural factors pull the other way, and both make a non-qualifying response the path of least resistance in a shock. First, both already have mature, means-tested national delivery systems: UK Universal Credit, and Canadian CRA refundable credits (CCB, CGEB). Second, their center-left mainstreams (UK Lib Dems' GBI, Scottish MIG, Canadian PBO/S-206 GLBI) favor income-tested floors. The UK has the most UBI-sympathetic head of government of any G7 country today (Burnham) but faces acute gilt-market and fiscal-rule constraints and a Reform-led polling threat for 2029. Canada has a stable, popular Liberal majority to 2029 whose leadership has de-prioritized basic income. AI exposure in both is comparable to the US (IMF: about 60% of advanced-economy jobs exposed; StatCan: about 60% of Canadian workers). Canada's adoption intensity is closer to the US than the UK's. Election-timing markets imply under 10% odds of an early election in either country before 2027. The model's 'other' category is large in both countries (hung or minority parliaments at about 0.45-0.5 next election); the rationales describe which coalitions sit inside it. countries.system_notes:
Federal parliamentary system. Each point below matters for how a cash benefit becomes law.
(1) The Chancellor needs a Bundestag majority, which in practice means a multi-party coalition bound by a coalition agreement. So a UBI needs every coalition partner, and the SPD, usually the senior partner on the left, formally rejects a basic income (BGE).
(2) The Bundesrat's consent is needed for laws touching taxes shared with the Länder, such as income tax and VAT, for laws obliging the Länder to make money payments, and for laws fixing Länder administrative procedure. The Bundesrat can only delay other laws, and the Bundestag can override it (https://www.bundesrat.de/DE/aufgaben/gesetzgebung/zust-einspr/zust-einspr-node.html). A UBI financed through income tax would almost certainly be a consent law, which gives state governments a veto.
(3) The Constitutional Court's subsistence-minimum (Existenzminimum) doctrine: its 5 Nov 2019 ruling (1 BvL 7/16) says the subsistence minimum must be guaranteed at all times (https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Entscheidungen/DE/2019/11/ls20191105_1bvl000716.html). A flat UBI below real needs, such as housing costs, would therefore still need means-tested top-ups, which raises its net cost.
(4) The debt brake (Schuldenbremse) was loosened in March 2025 by constitutional amendment with two-thirds of both chambers. It exempted defence above 1% of GDP and created a €500bn infrastructure fund (https://www.bundestag.de/dokumente/textarchiv/2025/kw12-de-sondersitzung-1056916). Deficit-financed recurring transfers still fall under the brake. A new exemption would need a two-thirds majority.
(5) Snap elections happen only after a lost confidence vote or a failed chancellor election (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_German_federal_election).
(6) Classification used here: left-led means an SPD, Green or Linke chancellor without the Union. Right-led means a Union-led government without SPD or Greens, which in practice needs AfD participation or toleration, or an AfD-led government. Cross-bloc coalitions (Union–SPD as now, Union–Greens, 'Kenya') and minority governments count as other, the analogue of US divided government.

countries.left_bloc: SPD, Greens (Bündnis 90/Die Grünen) and Die Linke. Treat this bloc as the more UBI-receptive camp. The Greens' 2020 basic programme adopted the unconditional basic income as a 'Leitidee' (guiding idea), against the leadership's wishes. Die Linke's members voted 56.6% for adding a BGE in 2022. Their voters are the most pro-UBI. Two brakes: the SPD, normally the senior partner, rejects BGE as 'wrong' (2019), and Linke delegates overrode the member vote in October 2024. Current polling (Sept 2026) has the three at roughly 38–42% combined, well short of a majority (https://www.wahlrecht.de/umfragen/). Left governments are forming at state level: a SPD–Linke–Greens coalition is expected in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Die Linke won Berlin.
countries.right_bloc: CDU/CSU and AfD (FDP and BSW are near or below the 5% threshold). The Union drove the 2026 tightening of the basic benefit (Grundsicherung): more sanctions and no asset grace period. In 2024 the AfD rejected a BGE for 'work refusers' in favour of an 'activating' benefit with community work. In 2020, however, it floated a €500/month citizens-only 'Staatsbürgergeld', a welfare-chauvinist near-UBI that would satisfy a citizens-only qualifying definition. The Union's firewall against the AfD is eroding: 51% (and 55% of Union voters) say parties should not rule out AfD cooperation (YouGov, Sept 2026).

p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: Left-led here means an SPD, Green or Linke chancellor without the Union. September 2026 polls put SPD+Greens+Linke at about 38–42% (Forsa 42, INSA 39, YouGov 39), against AfD+Union at about 45–51% (wahlrecht.de). Kalshi prices SPD at 4¢ and Greens at 3¢ to win the most seats. Polymarket left-wing chancellors before 2028 sum to about 15%, but those markets are thin and include in-term successions. The Union's collapse (4.9% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) and Linke's Berlin win show high volatility, hence the upper tail. The next election is due January–March 2029, or earlier through a snap election.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: Right-led here means a Union-led government without SPD or Greens (which in practice needs the AfD) or an AfD-led government. Evidence: AfD+Union hold a clear majority in every September 2026 poll, and Kalshi gives the AfD 81% to win the most seats. Voters are dropping the firewall: 51% overall and 55% of Union voters (YouGov, Sept 2026). On the other side, the CDU leadership still rules out the AfD; Merz accused it of 'ethnic cleansing' on 9 Sep 2026. The remaining ~0.64 is 'other', meaning cross-bloc coalitions like today's Union–SPD, Kenya-style coalitions or minority governments, which remain the modal outcome.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Over 2033+ elections the left's structural share (about 40% now) could recover, as in 2021 when the SPD led. Offsetting that, a durable AfD first place and eastern realignment (AfD 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt, 38.2% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) shrink the paths to a left majority. Wide range to reflect party-system flux.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: The chance of the firewall breaking rises with each cycle that the AfD leads, per YouGov's trend from 46% to 40% support for exclusion between August and September 2026. The upper tail is an AfD-led or Union–AfD government. The rest is cross-bloc coalitions.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta mode of 0.03. The SPD, the usual senior left partner, calls a BGE 'falsch' (2019). Linke delegates rejected a BGE in October 2024 despite the 57% member vote. The Greens hold a BGE only as a 'Leitidee' next to the means-tested Garantiesicherung. Hamburg voters rejected even a 2,000-person pilot, 62.7% to 37.3%, in October 2025. Positives: about 50–53% public support (Ipsos 2017, DIW 2022) and strong pilot evidence (DIW April 2025). Veto points: coalition partners, the Bundesrat for income-tax financing, and the subsistence-minimum rule, which forces top-ups to remain.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: The Union just led the March 2026 tightening of basic security. The AfD rejects a BGE for 'work refusers' (2024) and wants compulsory community work. The Union, the AfD and the SPD together voted down even a €320/yr Klimageld (March 2026).

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: In a shock, the Greens (with the BGE 'Leitidee') and the Linke base would push hard, public support is already about half, and pilot evidence is favourable. Fiscal room is moderate: 2025 deficit 2.4% of GDP, GDP €4.53tn, but the debt brake still binds on transfers. Discounted from the US mode of 0.45 for four reasons. First, coalitions need the SPD, which prefers raising Grundsicherung and unemployment insurance. Second, Bundesrat consent is needed for income-tax financing. Third, the subsistence-minimum doctrine forces a costly UBI plus top-ups. Fourth, a strong existing floor and short-time work give ready alternatives that do not qualify.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: The Union opposes a basic income. The AfD's 2020 €500 citizens-only Staatsbürgergeld shows a welfare-chauvinist near-UBI is thinkable, and it would meet a citizens-only qualifying definition, but by 2024 the party had moved to workfare. Near the low end of the US divided-government range.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: Cross-bloc coalitions do deliver consensus crisis cash. The 2022 €300 energy payment to all taxable workers and pensioners showed Germany can pay near-universal cash through payroll and pension channels. But a recurring statutory UBI needs the SPD to reverse its line and the Union to accept it. Comparable to the US divided-government range of 0.03–0.15.

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: The IMF (2024) finds about 60% of advanced-economy jobs exposed to AI, and the US has the highest mean exposure (World Bank/ILO-based index: US 62). The IAB finds rising substitution potential in expert occupations (36% of tasks in 2022). Lower than 1 because Germany's larger manufacturing base, dismissal protection, works councils and short-time work (general knowledge, not re-sourced this session) convert displacement into hours cuts rather than a measured unemployment jump of 3pp or more. The labour market is already weak (registered unemployment over 3m in January 2026), which can blur attribution to AI.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Multinational and English-language services adopt quickly, but codetermination, smaller firm AI budgets and slower European adoption delay displacement. Unemployment insurance (ALG I) also delays the measured unemployment peak.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: 2025 GDP per capita is €54,240 (Destatis). Benchmarks as a share of it: the Grundsicherungsgeld standard rate of €563/month (€6,756/yr) is 12.5%; the AfD Staatsbürgergeld of €500/month is 11.1%; Mein Grundeinkommen's €1,200/month is 26.5%, the level where DIW survey support peaks; the Klimageld of €320/yr is 0.6%. A normal-times enactment would most plausibly replace the basic benefit near subsistence, or be a partial/dividend design.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: A shock raises political pressure for a subsistence-level floor paid to all: 12.5% for the standard rate alone, more with a housing allowance. Upper tail: the €1,200 pilot level (26.5%). Lower tail: a partial payment topped up by means-tested aid.

countries.system_notes:
Semi-presidential unitary state. How a cash benefit becomes law:
(1) When the President and the Assembly majority are aligned, the executive dominates. Government bills pass by Assembly majority, and after a failed joint committee (CMP) the government can give the Assembly the final word over the Senate (Art. 45). Finance and social-security financing bills can pass under Art. 49.3 unless a censure motion succeeds (https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/le-bloc-de-constitutionnalite/texte-integral-de-la-constitution-du-4-octobre-1958-en-vigueur).
(2) Article 40 bars private members' bills and amendments that create or raise a public charge. A UBI therefore has to come as a government bill, so the executive is the real gatekeeper (https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_40_de_la_Constitution_de_la_Cinqui%C3%A8me_R%C3%A9publique_fran%C3%A7aise).
(3) The President may dissolve the Assembly, but not twice within a year (Art. 12). A new president in May 2027 would be expected to dissolve for a majority. Public Sénat notes a legal debate over whether any dissolution shortly before the handover constrains the successor (https://www.publicsenat.fr/actualites/politique/nouvelle-dissolution-avant-la-presidentielle-2027-une-instrumentalisation-de-la-constitution-que-rien-ninterdit).
(4) Cohabitation, a President facing a hostile Assembly, shifts domestic policy to the PM, and minority governments like today's can barely pass budgets.
(5) The départements finance and run the RSA, and a 2019 bill to let them experiment with a basic income was rejected.
(6) Fiscal constraint is severe: 2025 deficit 5.1% of GDP, debt 115.6%, compulsory levies 43.6%, public spending 57.2% (https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/8956575), under EU fiscal-rule pressure.
(7) Classification used here: left-led means a left president (LFI, PS/Place publique, Écologistes, PCF) with an aligned government, or a left PM. Right-led means an RN or LR-aligned president with an aligned government. Centrist presidents (Philippe, Attal), cohabitations and minority governments count as other.

p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: The next period starts with the April–May 2027 presidential election and the probable post-election legislative election. Polymarket puts the left's chance of winning the presidency at about 22.6% (Mélenchon 14.5, Hollande 5.45, Glucksmann 1.65, others). Runoff polls are poor for Mélenchon (31 vs Le Pen 69, Harris Sept 2026). The United Left primary looks likely to be cancelled (92%), a sign of fragmentation. Conditional on a left president, I put about 0.6 on getting an aligned Assembly government after dissolution, plus a small chance of a left PM under a non-left president.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: Polymarket: Le Pen 42.75% to win and 88.5% to reach the runoff. She leads every tested runoff (57–43 against Philippe). The right-wing total is about 56% including Lisnard, Retailleau, Bardella, Zemmour and Knafo. Discounted for the risk of an RN or LR president failing to win an aligned Assembly majority, and for Le Pen's pending cassation appeal. Centrist wins (Philippe 18.5%, Attal 2%) and cohabitations count as 'other' (about 0.45).

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: France alternates. A right or RN government elected in 2027 facing an unpopular fiscal squeeze would raise the left's odds in 2032. The left bloc is historically about a third of the vote, but it is split between LFI and the PS.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: The RN has become the dominant single party (the Senate group is new in 2026). Its long-run odds depend on how the 2027 outcome plays out.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: France has a real UBI lineage: Hamon in 2017 and 18 départements backing the 2019 experiment bill. Once president and Assembly are aligned there are few veto points: the Assembly has the last word, Art. 49.3 is available, and Art. 40 is no obstacle to a government bill, and the term is five years. But current left platforms are means-tested (LFI's poverty-line guarantee, Ruffin's RSA for under-25s, the Greens' means-tested revenu citoyen in 2022). Representative polling is cool toward a true UBI (OpinionWay 2018: 63% against; Ipsos 2017: 29% support). The fiscal position is very tight: deficit 5.1%, debt 115.6%.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: The RN proposed only targeted benefits in 2022 and a €125bn savings plan in 2026. LR voters are the most hostile (40% even for a means-tested version). Only 16–21% of Fillon and Le Pen voters were favourable in 2018.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: An aligned left executive faces fewer veto points than a German coalition and has five years instead of four. The UBI idea is well known, and Hamon and Mélenchon voters are sympathetic. But the left's reflex is a poverty-line top-up, which would not qualify. Bond-market and EU-rule constraints bind hard at 115.6% debt. Unemployment was already rising to 8.3% in Q2 2026. Overall similar to or slightly below the US D-trifecta mode of 0.45 after these discounts.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: The RN is welfare-chauvinist, not pro-UBI. A 'national preference' cash transfer is conceivable in a crisis and would meet a citizens-only definition, but there is no evidence it is planned. LR opposes. Comparable to the low end of the US divided-government range.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: Centrist and minority governments reach for technocratic means-tested consolidation, such as the allocation sociale unique merging the RSA, prime d'activité and APL, rather than universality. The fragmented Assembly barely passes budgets (Polymarket 38% for a budget by 31 Dec 2026).

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: The IMF (2024) finds about 60% of advanced-economy jobs exposed, and the US has the highest mean exposure. France's services-heavy economy is exposed, but strict employment protection and a large public sector (general knowledge, not re-sourced this session) slow layoffs. Unemployment is already 8.3% (Q2 2026, up 0.7pp year on year), so a shock would compound existing weakness, but attributing it to AI may be contested.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: European enterprise AI adoption lags the US. Labour-law and consultation procedures delay mass layoffs, and unemployment insurance delays the measured peak.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: GDP per capita is about €43,300, derived from 2025 GDP of about €2,994bn (Insee debt ratio) divided by about 69.2m people. As a share of that: the RSA of €651.69/month (€7,820/yr) is 18%; Hamon's €750 is 20.8%; the €600–800 tested by OpinionWay is 17–22%; the €800 petition level is 22%. Severe fiscal constraint pushes a normal-times design toward a partial UBI below the RSA.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: A shock pushes toward an RSA-level floor for everyone (about 18%), but debt of 115.6% of GDP caps generosity. Upper tail: Hamon or the €1,200 petition target (about 33%) is unlikely.

cross_country.notes: Both countries have stronger means-tested floors, stronger employment protection and weaker UBI momentum than the headline polls suggest. Germany's 2026 reform tightened conditionality. France's live reform, the allocation sociale unique, is means-tested consolidation. The most revealing real-world test, the Hamburg referendum of October 2025, rejected even a pilot, 62.7% to 37.3%. For the model: (a) treat cross-bloc coalitions (Germany) and centrist or cohabitation governments (France) as 'other'. (b) Both countries' left blocs lean toward poverty-line top-ups rather than universal payments, so q_left stays below the US D-trifecta values even in a shock, except where France's majoritarian executive offsets this. (c) The citizens-only qualifying definition means a welfare-chauvinist right (AfD's 2020 €500 Staatsbürgergeld, a hypothetical RN national-preference benefit) has a small but non-zero route to a qualifying program. (d) There are no UBI-specific prediction markets for either country; election markets from Polymarket and Kalshi were pulled from public APIs on 29–30 Sep 2026. The web-search budget ran out during research, so recent (2025–26) representative UBI polling is a gap for both countries.

input_objections.problem: The rationale's premise that the US has the highest mean exposure is contradicted by the cited IMF note. Kurzarbeit is time-limited and suits cyclical shocks, not sustained structural displacement, so a mode of 0.6 over-discounts a sustained shock.

verification.summary:
I checked 66 fields: 48 confirmed, 12 corrected, 2 wrong and 4 unverifiable. My web-search budget was already used up, so every check comes from pages I fetched directly or from the public Polymarket, Kalshi and Wikipedia APIs.

**Confirmed:**
- **Germany:**
  - Government and crisis: Merz is chancellor and the coalition holds 328 of 630 seats. The state results (CDU 17.2%, 4.9%, Linke first in Berlin) and the INSA and YouGov numbers are right.
  - Markets and dates: every Kalshi price and volume matches, as does the 2029 election window.
  - Positions and programs: the Linke member vote, the Halle congress, AfD 2024, the Grundsicherung vote (320-268, 5 Mar 2026) and €563 rate, the Klimageld vote, the DIW pilot, Hamburg, Destatis GDP per capita (€54,240), the BVerfG ruling, the Bundesrat rules and the debt brake are right.
- **France:**
  - Government and elections: the Lecornu II minority (211 of 577 seats), the Senate result, the Le Pen appeal and cassation timing, and the 2027 dates are right.
  - Markets: every Polymarket presidential, second-round, left-primary and PS-nominee price is right.
  - Polls, programs and finances: OpinionWay 2018, Ifop 2021, Ipsos, Info.fr, Hamon at 6.36%, the RSA at €651.69, the allocation sociale unique, the AI petition and the Insee fiscal figures are right.

**Errors to fix:**
1. **French poll numbers mix scenarios.** Harris 22-24 Sep has Attal at 5%, not 10%. Cluster17 has no Attal in its scenario with Philippe; the researcher's 'Attal 12' blends two scenarios (Attal is 13.5% in the other one).
2. **ESS France is wrong.** France reads about 49.7% on Figure 6, just below 50, not 52-54%. The cross-country claim that France is above 50% is also wrong.
3. **Greens and left-bloc ranges are too narrow.** Greens ran 13-18% in September, not 14-16%. The left bloc ran about 36-42%, not 38-42%.
4. **Lecornu market.** It is 11.55%, not 11.25%, and it prices him being the next listed leader out, not the chance he leaves office.
5. **AfD Staatsbürgergeld is overstated as citizens-only.** Non-citizens could qualify after 10 years of taxable income, and higher earners would get a tax cut instead of cash.
6. **SPD 'December 2019 resolution'** is not supported by the cited source, which is the executive paper of February 2019.
7. **Klimageld citation.** The claim that it is missing from the 2025 coalition agreement is correct against the agreement's own text, but the cited article says the opposite. The citation should point to the agreement.
8. **AI-exposure premise is wrong.** The IMF note puts the UK (about 70%) above the US (about 60%, the advanced-economy average), so the US does not have the highest exposure.
9. **Medef debate summary** misstates Le Pen's retirement pledge (only for early starters) and Glucksmann's tax proposal.

**Input objections:**
- **Missing input:** there is no q_enact_per_term_other_normal for either country, even though 'other' is the most likely government type.
- **France left AI-shock mode:** the rationale calls 0.28 'similar to' the US 0.45. It also ignores that France's 5-year term should scale the probability up.
- **Germany right-led mode:** 0.28 is rich given that the CDU refused the AfD even in Saxony-Anhalt, and the markets are thin (Kalshi Weidel 16¢). I suggest a mode of 0.19.
- **AI exposure for both countries:** 0.6 over-discounts once the US-highest premise is dropped. I suggest 0.7 for Germany and 0.75 for France.

The other ranges look reasonable against the evidence and the US scale.

**Unverifiable:** the Greens' 62% delegate share, the PS primary dates of 9 and 17 Oct, France's 8.3% unemployment and 69.2m population, and Germany's 2.4% deficit, IAB and 3m-unemployment figures. No source was given and I could not fetch one.

countries.governing_parties_and_majority: A PSOE–Sumar minority coalition. Wikipedia lists PSOE at 121 seats and Sumar and allies at 26, well short of 176 of 350 in the Congress of Deputies. The coalition depends on case-by-case votes from regionalist and left parties. Junts (7 seats) withdrew support in October 2025 but has not backed a no-confidence motion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Spanish_general_election). The PP has held an absolute majority in the Senate since 2023: 143 of 266 seats at constitution (https://www.vozpopuli.com/politica/elecciones-generales-2023/mayoria-absoluta-pp-senado.html). The 2023 budget is still in force after three extensions, and the 2027 budget missed the 30 September constitutional deadline for submission (https://www.esdiario.com/nacional/260929/198924/sanchez-agota-legislatura-cuentas-2023-cuatro-anos-pais-presupuestos.html; https://www.cronista.com/espana/economia-finanzas/presupuestos-2027-hacienda-promete-llevarlos-al-congreso-este-ano-y-negociara-con-todos-los-grupos/).
countries.system_notes: Parliamentary monarchy with asymmetric bicameralism. A national cash benefit is a Social Security or state competence. The IMV template was a government Real Decreto-ley, which Congress validates, and was later processed as Ley 19/2021 (https://www.seg-social.es/wps/portal/wss/internet/Trabajadores/PrestacionesPensionesTrabajadores/65850d68-8d06-4645-bde7-05374ee42ac7). The Senate can veto or amend within 2 months, or 20 days if the bill is urgent. Congress overrides by absolute majority (176) immediately, or by simple majority after 2 months (Art. 90: https://app.congreso.es/consti/constitucion/indice/sinopsis/sinopsis.jsp?art=90&tipo=2). A PP-controlled Senate can therefore delay but not block. The real veto point is a fragmented Congress where no bloc has 176. Every left-led government since 2018 has needed Junts, PNV, ERC, Bildu and others; Junts and PNV are centre-right on fiscal matters. Budget passage is a separate hurdle: none has passed since 2023. Autonomous communities run their own minimum-income schemes, and Catalonia designed its own UBI pilot. Fiscal room: general-government debt was 101% of GDP in April 2026 (https://www.bde.es/wbe/es/noticias-eventos/actualidad-banco-espana/deuda-aapp-abril26.html). The 2025 deficit was 2.2% of GDP (https://www.hacienda.gob.es/es-ES/Prensa/Noticias/Paginas/2026/20260331-NP-CIERRE-DEFICIT.aspx), and EU fiscal rules apply. For scale: GDP per capita was about €34,210 in 2025 (INE/Eurostat per search result, https://www.ine.es/dyngs/Prensa/CNA2025.htm). The US threshold of 6.7% of GDP per capita is about €2,290 per adult per year, or roughly €190 a month.

countries.left_bloc: A PSOE-led government: PSOE plus Sumar, relying on Podemos, ERC, EH Bildu, BNG and similar parties. Treat it as the more UBI-receptive camp because its junior partners favour UBI. Movimiento Sumar (Nov 2025) proposed a universal €550/month income for 18- to 21-year-olds as a 'starting point' toward a citizens' basic income for everyone. Podemos has put UBI in manifestos. ERC designed the Catalan UBI pilot. PSOE itself is not pro-UBI. It built the means-tested IMV and presents that as its answer, and Sumar's 2023 universal inheritance was dropped in the coalition pact with Sánchez. Left receptivity therefore depends on how much leverage the junior partners have.

p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: All private September 2026 polls show PP ahead of PSOE by 6-8.5 pp, with PP+Vox around 50% of the vote and over 176 seats in most projections (SocioMétrica 207, DYM about 202-209). Polymarket gives Feijóo 79% to be the next PM. The CIS (PSOE +5.5) is a known outlier. I keep 20% rather than lower because 2023 set a precedent: PP won a plurality but PSOE governed with regionalist support. Vox dependence can also mobilize anti-PP partners.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: This mirrors the Polymarket Feijóo price (79%) and polls showing a PP+Vox seat majority. It leaves about 4% for 'other' outcomes: a grand coalition, a technocratic or caretaker government, or a repeat election.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Since 2018 Spain has alternated between PSOE and PP governments, with PSOE governing longer. After a likely PP term from 2027, alternation pushes the left share back toward about 45%. The fragmented left (Sumar at 4.5-7%, Podemos at 1-3%) makes a PSOE-led majority harder than in the past.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Symmetric to the left, with a slight structural edge from the combined PP+Vox vote of about 50% in current polling. The remaining 5% is 'other'.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Comparable to the US D-trifecta normal mode of 0.03, but lower. PSOE owns the means-tested IMV and presents it as its answer. It dropped Sumar's universal inheritance in 2023, and its AI plan (IA360) offers social dialogue and an observatory, not income. Spanish left governments are minorities needing Junts or PNV, no budget has passed since 2023, debt is 101% of GDP and EU fiscal rules bind. Upside: Sumar's youth UBI proposal and the IMV administrative infrastructure.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: I found no national UBI position from PP or Vox. Both voted in Catalonia (2023) to strike even the UBI pilot's budget article. A PP government would likely rely on Vox, which has no UBI position I could verify.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta shock mode of 0.45. Spanish left governments are never single-party majorities, so they need Junts or PNV, who are fiscally centre-right and voted against the Catalan pilot. PSOE's default shock response is to expand the means-tested IMV and job-retention schemes rather than a universal payment. EU fiscal rules and 101% debt also bind. In a shock, however, Sumar's explicit youth-UBI-as-first-step framing, historical support of 52-69% in polls, and an existing IMV payment rail make a universal extension plausible. The Senate can only delay (Art. 90).

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: Roughly the low end of the US divided-shock range of 0.03-0.15. A PP government, likely dependent on Vox, would more plausibly expand the IMV or tax credits. It keeps some chance because a large shock with unemployment already near 10% could force a broad cash response, and the PP-controlled Senate would not be an obstacle.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: Covers a grand coalition, technocratic or caretaker government. A PP–PSOE arrangement would likely compromise on an IMV expansion; universal cash is possible only in a severe shock. Placed mid-range relative to the US divided-government shock band of 0.03-0.15.

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: Funcas (April 2026) puts Spain's generative-AI workforce exposure at 27.4%, slightly above the OECD's 26%. It estimates automation risk at only 5.9% against 12% for the OECD, because Spanish jobs involve more interpersonal and physical tasks such as tourism and hospitality. Its central scenario is a net loss of about 400K jobs over ten years (1.7-2.3M gross). Only 21.1% of firms used AI in Q1 2025. The IMF puts US high-exposure employment near 60%. So a US-scale shock plausibly reaches Spain, but with a smaller displacement per unit of AI capability.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Firm adoption lags the US (21.1% of firms in Q1 2025), and EU AI Act and regulatory frictions may slow deployment (see IMF WP/25/67 on regulation in Europe). Offsetting this, 44.2% of working-age Spaniards already use generative AI according to Plan IA360, and back-office and administrative roles, the most exposed per Funcas, can be offshored or automated quickly.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: Spanish reference amounts are high relative to GDP per capita (about €34,210): the IMV single-adult guarantee is 26%, Sumar's youth income 19% and the Catalan pilot 28%. A national universal payment enacted without a shock would likely be a partial UBI, since each 1% of GDP per capita per adult costs about 0.8% of GDP. One VAT-financed design discussed is €400/month, about 14%. The US threshold of 6.7% equals about €190/month, so most plausible enactments clear it.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: In a shock the amount would move toward the IMV and poverty-line anchors of 19-28% of GDP per capita that Spanish proposals use, capped by debt and EU fiscal rules. The mode matches the €400/month VAT-financed design (14%).

key_risks: The 2027 election, due by 2027-08-22 and possibly earlier in Feb/Mar 2027 if the budget fails, very likely produces a PP-led government dependent on Vox, which would pause UBI-receptive government for one or two terms.

Policy substitution: the Spanish left's instinct in a shock is to expand the means-tested IMV and job-retention schemes rather than pay a universal benefit, so a shock may be absorbed without a qualifying UBI.
Fragmented Congress: left governments need Junts or PNV, who are fiscally conservative on transfers; Junts voted to strike the Catalan pilot. No budget has passed since 2023.
Fiscal constraints: debt of 101% of GDP, a 2.2% deficit and EU fiscal rules. A threshold-level UBI of 6.7% of GDP per capita per adult costs roughly 5-6% of GDP.
Measured AI automation risk is lower than the OECD's (5.9% vs 12%), so the shock may be smaller or slower in Spain.
The CIS house effect could mislead: it shows PSOE ahead while private pollsters show PP ahead.
Regional pilots (Catalonia) could be revived under a different Generalitat, but they are regional and do not qualify.
unknowns: No Spain-specific UBI poll from 2024-2026 was found; the latest are YouGov (2022) and Dalia (2017). A European Social Survey 2016 Spain figure of about 50% appeared only in a search summary and was not verified.
PP and Vox national positions on UBI: no explicit statement found. The inference rests on the Catalan 2023 vote and the absence of any proposal.
Whether Podemos has a live UBI bill in the XV legislature: none found.
IMV annual cost: only monthly spending (€465.7M in June 2026) was verified; the annualized figure of about €5.6bn is my arithmetic.
Spain's adult (18+) population share, used for the cost arithmetic of roughly 0.8-0.85 of the population, was assumed, not verified.
No IMF country-level high-exposure employment share for Spain (comparable to the US's 60%) was found; the Funcas and OECD exposure measure uses a different methodology.
The Polymarket 'Next Prime Minister of Spain' price was read from the Spain predictions hub; the event page itself returned no data.
Whether and when the 2027 budget will be tabled, and its fate, are uncertain; this drives the snap-election timing.

countries.head_of_government: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), President (head of state and government). He is running for re-election on 2026-10-04 with Geraldo Alckmin as running mate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Brazilian_general_election).
countries.governing_parties_and_majority: A PT-led presidency without a reliable congressional majority. Lula's 2026 coalition, 'Brasil Pronto para Mais', includes the Brazil of Hope federation (PT, PCdoB, PV), the PSOL-REDE federation, PSB and PDT. In the 513-seat Chamber, the largest blocs are PL (98), UPB (98) and Brazil of Hope (81), followed by PSD (48) and Republicanos (42). All 513 Chamber seats and 54 of 81 Senate seats are up on 2026-10-04 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Brazilian_general_election). Projections have the right holding at least 40 of 81 Senate seats from 2027, close to or at an absolute majority (https://www.congressoemfoco.com.br/noticia/119663/direita-deve-ter-ao-menos-40-das-81-cadeiras-no-senado-em-2027).
countries.system_notes: Presidential federal republic with a bicameral Congress. A national cash benefit needs an ordinary law passed by both houses and sanctioned by the president. A presidential veto falls only with an absolute majority in each house counted separately: 257 deputies and 41 senators (https://www.congressonacional.leg.br/materias/vetos/entenda-a-tramitacao-do-veto). Key specifics: (1) Law 10.835/2004 already creates a universal Renda Básica de Cidadania for Brazilians and foreigners resident 5+ years, regardless of socioeconomic condition. It is to be phased in, with the Executive setting the amount, but it has only ever been implemented partially (https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renda_b%C3%A1sica_universal). A qualifying UBI could therefore be reached by an executive regulation of an existing statute plus budget appropriations, without a new statute. (2) Constitutional Amendment 114/2021 added to Art. 6 a right to a 'family basic income' for the socially vulnerable, subject to fiscal and budget law (https://www2.camara.leg.br/legin/fed/emecon/2021/emendaconstitucional-114-16-dezembro-2021-792108-publicacaooriginal-164118-pl.html). (3) Lei 14.601/2023 declares Bolsa Família a stage in the gradual universalization of the RBC (https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2023-2026/2023/lei/l14601.htm). (4) In MI 7300 (2021), the Supreme Court ordered the first phase of the RBC for the poor from 2022 and still supervises it (https://portal.stf.jus.br/noticias/verNoticiaDetalhe.asp?idConteudo=464858&ori=1). (5) Electoral law bars new free benefits in election years unless already authorized by law and executed in the prior year (Lei 9.504 art. 73 §10), so new programmes cluster in odd years (https://temasselecionados.tse.jus.br/temas-selecionados/condutas-vedadas-a-agentes-publicos/distribuicao-gratuita-de-bens-valores-ou-beneficios). (6) The 2023 fiscal framework caps real spending growth and sets primary-balance targets: +0.25% of GDP in 2026, but the forecast is a deficit of 0.59% (https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/brazil-widens-2026-primary-deficit-forecast-to-1561-billion-4915549). Gross debt is projected at 83.7% of GDP at end-2026, rising to 89.7% by 2030 (https://www.riotimesonline.com/brazil-public-debt-projection-2030-september-2026/). The right has used constitutional amendments to raise cash transfers before elections (PEC 15/2022, Auxílio Brasil at R$600). GDP per capita was R$59,687 in 2025, so the US 6.7% threshold is about R$4,000 per adult per year, or R$333 a month (https://www.dgabc.com.br/Noticia/4288338/pib-per-capita-sobe-a-rs-59-687-49-em-2025-e-e-o-maior-da-serie-revela-ibge).

countries.left_bloc: A PT-led presidency (Lula, with PT/PCdoB/PV, PSOL-REDE, PSB, PDT). This is the UBI-receptive camp. PT's Eduardo Suplicy authored Law 10.835/2004. The Lula government's 2023 Bolsa Família law frames the programme as a stage toward universal RBC. Suplicy, now a PT state deputy running again in 2026, lobbies for the transition. But Lula's 2026 plan proposes expanding Bolsa Família (extra child benefits) rather than a universal RBC. Any left president faces a centrão- and right-dominated Congress, so 'left-led' here means a left executive with a hostile or transactional legislature.
countries.right_bloc: A PL or Bolsonaro-led presidency (Flávio Bolsonaro, with Alfredo Gaspar), or another right candidate such as Caiado (PSD), Zema (NOVO) or Renan Santos (Missão). The right promises to keep Bolsa Família but reframe it as temporary, with an 'exit door' into work. Zema proposes work or study requirements and Renan Santos would replace it with work-based assistance. The Brazilian right is not averse to cash, however: Bolsonaro's government created Auxílio Brasil and raised it to R$600 by constitutional amendment in the 2022 election year. A centrist 'other' president, such as Augusto Cury (Avante), is a small probability.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: The complement of the left estimate minus about 2% for a centrist 'other' winner such as Cury, whom polls put at 5-10% in the first round but markets price below 1%. Markets show Flávio pulling ahead since 2026-09-11.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: The left's post-Lula succession is untested; see unknowns on eligibility and age. The right is structurally strengthening: projections have it near a Senate majority and PL the largest Chamber bloc. The PT has won 5 of the last 6 presidential races before 2026, so I keep a substantial but below-even share.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: The right has a growing congressional base and markets currently favour it. The remaining 12% covers centrist or 'other' presidents, a real possibility in Brazil's fragmented system.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Unique upside: the universal statute (Law 10.835) already exists, the Bolsa Família law calls itself a stage toward universalization, and EC 114/STF MI 7300 give a judicial hook. The Executive could in principle scale up the RBC by regulation with budget cover. But no 2026 plan mentions UBI, Lula proposes expanding targeted Bolsa Família, and the fiscal target is being missed (-0.59% vs +0.25% of GDP) with debt rising to about 90% of GDP. Congress controls appropriations. A threshold-level UBI would cost about 5% of GDP, roughly 4 times Bolsa Família's current annualized spending of about 1.2% of GDP (my arithmetic, assuming about 3/4 of the population is adult). Similar to the US D-trifecta normal mode of 0.03, slightly lower.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: Right candidates want time limits, exit doors or work requirements on Bolsa Família (Flávio, Zema, Caiado, Renan Santos). The right's willingness to raise cash transfers before elections (PEC 15/2022) keeps this slightly above the Spanish right, but such expansions have been targeted and temporary.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta shock mode of 0.45. A left president would face a right- or centrão-controlled Congress, a binding spending cap and a debt path already near 90% of GDP. Brazil's policy instinct is targeted transfers through CadÚnico, not universal ones. Offsetting upside: an existing universal statute, a constitutional basic-income right and an STF supervision channel make universalization legally 'shovel-ready', and the Suplicy/PT tradition supplies an agenda. Enactment windows are mainly in odd years because of the election-year benefit ban.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: The Brazilian right has shown it will use constitutional amendments to raise cash transfers under pressure (Auxílio Brasil R$600 in 2022), and it would control Congress. This is the upper part of the US divided-shock band (0.03-0.15). It is capped because its 2026 platforms stress work conditionality and exit doors, which runs against a universal, no-work-test design.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: A centrist president governing with the centrão would be transactional and could back a broad cash response in a severe shock, as Congress did with pandemic-era transfers, but would prefer targeted designs. Mid-range of the US divided-shock band.

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: The IMF (Cazzaniga et al. 2024) puts Brazil's high-exposure employment at 41%, against about 60% in the US and 70% in the UK, with Brazil 'a broadly intermediate case'. A large informal sector and lower wages reduce automation incentives and measured displacement. The IMF finds Brazilian workers leaving high-exposure jobs face wage losses, so exposed white-collar workers could be hit. The probability that a US-scale shock (3+ pp of unemployment) lands at comparable size is well below 0.5.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Adoption lag of an emerging market: lower capital intensity, informality, and a government AI plan (PBIA) focused on building sovereign capacity rather than rapid deployment. Offshored services such as call centres and back office could transmit a shock quickly, so the lower bound is 0.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: Brazilian reference amounts are low relative to GDP per capita (R$59,687). Bolsa Família's per-person component of R$142/month is 2.9% and Maricá's R$230/month is 4.6%. An IMF Fiscal Monitor scenario at 25% of median per-capita income was R$1,286/yr on 2013 data and cost 4.6% of GDP. A first universal RBC would likely be at or below these levels. The US 6.7% threshold (R$333/month per adult) may not be met even if a universal RBC is enacted.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: A shock-era programme would scale toward pandemic and election-year transfer levels; Auxílio Brasil paid R$600 per family. It is capped by a threshold-level UBI costing about 5% of GDP under a binding spending cap. The mode sits just below the US-equivalent threshold.

key_risks: The 2026-10-04/25 election is close to a coin flip: polls lean Lula in the runoff while markets favour Flávio at about 58%. A right-led 2027-2030 term delays any UBI-receptive executive to 2031 at the earliest.

Congress is the binding veto point for any president: the right is projected near an absolute Senate majority and PL is the largest Chamber bloc. Appropriations and veto overrides (257 deputies and 41 senators) sit with Congress.

Fiscal: the primary-balance target is being missed (-0.59% vs +0.25% of GDP in 2026), debt is projected at about 90% of GDP by 2030, and the spending cap binds. A threshold-level UBI costs about 5% of GDP.
Amount risk: Brazilian basic-income designs cluster at 2-5% of GDP per capita, so a universal RBC could be enacted yet fail a 6.7%-of-GDP-per-capita threshold. Model the threshold choice explicitly.
Policy path dependence: 'universalization' may proceed as gradual expansion of the targeted Bolsa Família, never reaching 'essentially all adults'.
Electoral law bans new benefits in election years (Lei 9.504 art. 73 §10), shortening the effective enactment window to about 3 years per term.
Lower AI exposure (41% high-exposure employment vs about 60% in the US) and informality mean a shock may be smaller or later.
A judicial wildcard cuts both ways: STF supervision in MI 7300 could push expansion, but so far it has accepted Bolsa Família as compliance.

cross_country.notes: Spain and Brazil are both 4-year cycles where the more UBI-receptive camp is currently in office but likely to lose, or roughly even, at the next election: Spain in 2027 (Feijóo at 79% on Polymarket) and Brazil in 2026 (Flávio at about 58% in markets, runoff tied in polls). Both have a means-tested national floor that is the policy's natural substitute: the IMV in Spain and Bolsa Família in Brazil. Both have sub-national basic-income experiments that do not qualify (Catalonia's stalled pilot and Maricá's means-tested municipal RBC). They differ on amounts relative to GDP per capita. Spanish designs are anchored at 19-28% of GDP per capita (IMV 26%, Catalan pilot 28%, Sumar youth income 19%). Brazilian designs sit at 2-5% (Bolsa Família per-person component 2.9%, Maricá 4.6%). A single 6.7%-of-GDP-per-capita threshold is therefore easy to clear in Spain but may bind in Brazil. Brazil has an unusual legal shortcut: a universal statute (Law 10.835/2004) already exists, backed by a constitutional right (EC 114/2021) and Supreme Court supervision (MI 7300). Universalization could come by executive regulation plus appropriations rather than a new law. Veto points: Spain's Senate can only delay, so the binding constraint is assembling 176 in a fragmented Congress. Brazil's binding constraint is a centrão- and right-leaning Congress controlling appropriations under a spending cap. AI exposure relative to the US is lower in both: Brazil has 41% high-exposure employment against about 60% in the US (IMF 2024), and Spain's automation risk is 5.9% against the OECD's 12% (Funcas 2026). Brazil sits lower and later.

input_objections.problem: A mode of 0.20 with a high of 0.42 sits above the whole US divided-government shock band (0.03-0.15), yet the researcher's own description of a Lula-type term is a left executive with a hostile Congress. The right is projected at 40 of 81 senators, PL and UPB hold 196 of 513 deputies, and Congress controls appropriations and veto overrides. Under the model's taxonomy (left-led / right-led / other including divided), that is structurally the divided case. The 'shovel-ready statute' upside is weaker than stated: Law 10.835 Art. 2 binds the Executive to Fiscal Responsibility Law arts. 16-17, so it needs fiscal compensation as well as appropriations, under a spending cap and debt heading to 89.7% of GDP. Either recode a left president without a congressional majority as 'other', or keep it left-led with a divided-style discount.

Auxílio Emergencial paid R$600/month per eligible adult (R$1,200 for single mothers) to about 68M people, which is 12% of 2025 GDP per capita even in nominal terms and far more in 2020 terms. The Bolsa Família family floor is now R$691 (a 15.04% readjustment). A shock-era enactment could land above the 6.7% threshold more often than this distribution implies, though fiscal limits on a lasting universal payment (about 0.75-0.8% of GDP per point of GDP per capita) argue against going as high as the temporary precedent.

input_objections.problem: The rationale (and system_notes and cross_country) treat 176 as the binding hurdle and say left governments 'need Junts or PNV'. Under Art. 79.2 an ordinary law passes by a majority of members present. A decree-law, the route the IMV used, needs only a Congress validation vote, and the PP Senate can delay an ordinary law by only 2 months (simple-majority override afterwards). Abstentions by Junts or PNV are enough, so this discount is overstated. The mode of 0.22 can stand because PSOE's own preference for the IMV and EU fiscal rules remain the real brakes, but the rationale should be corrected, and the high of 0.45 (equal to the US D-trifecta mode) should be justified by the decree-law channel rather than capped by a phantom 176 constraint.

The shock mode of 14% is anchored on a '€400/month VAT-financed design' that has no source. GDP per capita should also be €34,365 (INE, 2026-09-18), not €34,210; the threshold becomes about €2,302/yr (€192/month). The ranges are otherwise consistent with verified anchors (IMV 25.6%, Sumar youth income 19.2%, Catalan pilot 27.9%). Replace the unsourced anchor or cite it; no numeric change is required.

The researcher JSON is mostly accurate: 45 confirmed, 12 corrected, 1 wrong, 4 unverifiable. All 40dB, CIS, SocioMétrica, DYM, YouGov, Dalia and Polymarket figures matched exactly; Plan IA360 and the IMV figures matched. Funcas exposure figures and the €400/month design are unsourced. Brazil: WRONG that the new term starts 1 January; it starts 5 January (from 2027). The fiscal 'miss' is overstated: the headline deficit is 0.59% of GDP (R$80.9bn; the URL's '1561' is US$15.61bn), but the target-relevant figure is -0.1%. The right's Senate projection is 40 seats, one short of a majority (June 2026). Maricá's family count and oil-royalty funding are unsourced. All Brazil polls, Polymarket and Kalshi prices, Lei 14.601 Art. 1 §1, Law 10.835 text (which ties implementation to Fiscal Responsibility Law offsets), EC 114, IMF 41%/60%/70% exposure, and the Bolsa Família R$691 and 15.04% readjustment verified. Brazil's shock amount distribution omits the Auxílio Emergencial precedent (R$600 per adult to about 68M people, passed in about a week), so I suggest a mode of 7 and a high of 16. countries.system_notes: Presidential system with a unicameral 300-seat Assembly: 254 first-past-the-post seats and 46 PR seats, 4-year terms. The president serves one 5-year term with no re-election (Art. 70). Veto: the president returns a bill within 15 days, and the Assembly can override with two-thirds of members present (Art. 53). Budget: the Assembly cannot increase any expenditure item or create a new one without the Executive's consent (Art. 57, https://www.constituteproject.org/constitution/Republic_of_Korea_1987). So a national UBI needs both a willing president (the budget line) and an Assembly majority (the statute). Through June 2030 the president is DP, so the binding constraint is holding the Assembly after April 2028. The unitary state co-funds pilots with local government: the rural basic income pilot was split 40/30/30 national/province/county in 2026, with the national share rising to 50% in 2027. Constitutional amendment needs 200 of 300 votes plus a referendum. Lee backs a 4-year, two-term presidency, but a term change cannot benefit the incumbent (https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2026/08/16/politics-constitutional-amendment-presidency/3551786924282/). Precedent for universal cash exists as one-offs: 2020 disaster payments and the 2025 consumption coupons to all citizens. The recurring schemes Lee is known for paid in local-currency vouchers (지역화폐), which may fail the 'freely spendable cash' test. p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: The next election is the April 2028 Assembly vote. The DP president holds office through June 2030, so 'left-led' here means DP keeps a unified government (president plus Assembly majority), and a PPP-won Assembly would give divided ('other') government. The current period is already left-led: DP has 161 of 300 seats plus allies. For DP: Gallup Sept 2026 has DP at 40% vs PPP 27%, DP won 12 of 16 metropolitan races in June 2026, and DP took 161 constituency seats on about 51% of the constituency vote in 2024. Against: Lee's approval fell from 60% (Jan) to 37% (Sept, disapproval 56%), mostly over housing, DP lost Seoul, and Korean midterm-style Assembly elections often punish the sitting president. No prediction market on the 2028 Assembly exists.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: A PPP-led unified government cannot form before the March 2030 presidential election. The only path is Lee leaving early (Polymarket: 7% by end-2026), a PPP win in the snap election, and a PPP Assembly win. A PPP Assembly under Lee counts as 'other' (divided).

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: From 2030 on, the presidency is open (Lee is term-limited). Korea alternates: power changed hands in 2017, 2022 and 2025, and divided government is common (Yoon had a hostile Assembly throughout, and presidential and Assembly calendars are staggered). The 2030 frontrunners from each side (Kim Min-seok for DP, Jang Dong-hyeok for PPP) are within single digits in 2026 polling. I put the unified-DP share near 0.4, leaving about 0.3 for divided or other.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: PPP is weak after the martial-law crisis (21–27% support in 2026), but it held Seoul, Daegu and both Gyeongsangs in June 2026 and has won the presidency in alternation before. Needing both the presidency and an Assembly majority keeps this below the left share.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Higher than the US D-trifecta (0.03). Lee personally owns the idea. The state has a Basic Income Planning Team, a Basic Society Committee, and a cabinet plan naming basic income. Fiscal room is unusually large: debt about 52% of GDP (IMF), and the 2027 budget projects tax revenue up about 50% on the chip boom, with a new 162T-won Future Response Fund. Held down because the 2025 campaign dropped the UBI pledge, MoHW favours conditional 'participation income' pilots for youth and middle-aged adults, pension reform is moving toward targeting, and KIHASA 2024 found 54% opposed. Recurring Lee-style programs pay in local vouchers, which may fail the cash test. No basic income line appeared in the 2027 MoHW budget coverage I read. The 2028–30 window is Lee's lame-duck period.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: PPP supporters opposed Lee's UBI 89% (2021). The party attacks its financing as a tax burden. Its own floor model (Seoul 'safety income') is means-tested and would not qualify.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: About equal to the US D-trifecta in a shock. Upward: MoHW already justifies basic income by AI structural unemployment among youth, a ready policy apparatus exists, and a unified DP government in a unicameral legislature has no second chamber and a president who controls the budget (Art. 57). AI and chip rents are already swelling tax revenue, and universal one-off cash has been delivered twice (2020, 2025). Downward: the government keeps choosing conditional or voucher designs, only a 5-year presidency window exists, and the public is split roughly 46/54.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: A PPP government in a shock would most likely expand the means-tested 'safety income' (negative income tax) or one-off payments rather than a universal statute. Some chance comes from DP pressure in the Assembly and from precedent: the 2020 universal disaster payment happened under cross-party pressure.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: Divided government. A DP president (to 2030) with a PPP Assembly could propose but not pass the statute. A PPP president with a DP Assembly faces Art. 57: the Assembly cannot add new spending items without executive consent, and the president can veto (two-thirds to override). Emergency one-offs are likely; a lasting universal statute less so. Comparable to the upper half of the US divided-government range (0.03–0.15).

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: Korea is a highly digitised, tech-forward economy. Its government already describes AI-driven cuts to new hiring that hit youth first (MoHW, Apr 2026). Unemployment is 2.7% (World Bank 2025), with a similar starting slack to the US. It is not higher because the chip and AI boom is a large positive demand shock for Korea (2027 tax revenue up about 50%), and strong regular-worker protection and chaebol labour hoarding may show displacement as reduced hiring rather than a 3pp unemployment jump.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Fast tech adoption and an already visible youth hiring freeze argue for near-simultaneity. Some chance Korea leads by about a year. Labour-market rigidity could delay measured unemployment by a few years.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: Lee's own benchmarks are small. The 2022 pledge was 1M won/yr, about 1.9% of GDP per capita (2025 GDP per capita ₩51.5M, World Bank). The youth BI was 1M won, about 1.9%. The rural pilot pays 1.8M won/yr, about 3.5%. The child basic allowance pays 2.4M won/yr, about 4.7%. The Basic Income Party's 650k/month, about 15%, marks the far tail. A normal-times qualifying UBI would probably start as a small 'dividend', below the US 6.7% threshold.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: In a shock a DP government would likely scale toward the rural pilot and child allowance levels (3.5–4.7%) or higher, financed by AI and chip windfall taxes. Low debt (about 52% of GDP) allows more. The Basic Income Party's 15% bounds the top.

countries.system_notes: Parliamentary and unitary. A nationwide cash benefit needs a Diet statute plus budget appropriation. The House of Representatives has 4-year terms but can be dissolved early; the House of Councillors has 6-year terms with half elected every 3 years (Constitution Arts. 45–46). If the upper house rejects a bill, the lower house can pass it into law with a two-thirds vote (Art. 59, https://www.constituteproject.org/constitution/Japan_1946). The LDP alone (316 of 465) currently clears two-thirds, so the upper-house minority is not a hard veto until the next lower-house election. Budget and treaty procedures have separate lower-house-precedence rules (Art. 60–61; not re-verified in detail this session). Real veto points are intra-LDP factions and the LDP leadership vote (next in fall 2027), the Finance Ministry's fiscal stance with gross debt about 206% of GDP (IMF), and the coalition partner. Benefits are delivered by municipalities; the new worker credit is paid by city and ward heads on application. Universal one-off cash has precedent: ¥100,000 to every registered resident in 2020.

p_left_led_government_next_election.rationale: The next lower-house election is due by Feb 2030. The LDP holds 316 of 465 seats, and September 2026 party support is LDP 26–43% vs no other party above about 6–8%. The main opposition vehicle (CRA) collapsed on 17 Sep 2026. Takaichi's cabinet approval is 45–62%, and Polymarket gives 4–5% for her leaving in 2026 and 3% for a 2026 dissolution. A non-LDP government after the next election would need a historic reversal.

p_right_led_government_next_election.rationale: Same evidence. The residual (about 7%) is 'other': an LDP minority or loose-support government like Ishiba's in 2024–25, which is plausible if the LDP falls back from its 2026 peak. The July 2028 upper-house election could create a divided Diet, but the two-thirds override lasts only while the LDP keeps two-thirds of the lower house.

p_left_led_government_later_elections.rationale: Postwar base rate: non-LDP-led governments held office only in 1993–94 and 2009–12, about 6% of years. The opposition is currently reorganising (Democratic Reform Party, Komeito split off again), which could consolidate it later. Kept near the historical base rate.

p_right_led_government_later_elections.rationale: LDP dominance is the long-run norm, but 2024–25 showed the LDP can drop to minority status ('other'). Roughly 17% is left for minority or other arrangements.

q_enact_per_term_left_normal.rationale: Below the US D-trifecta (0.03). Japan's centre-left mainstream (CDP/DRP, Komeito) has pushed refundable credits and consumption-tax cuts, not UBI. Reiwa is marginal (1 lower-house seat). Non-LDP coalitions have been short-lived and fragile, and gross debt of about 206% of GDP (IMF) plus rising JGB yields limit fiscal room.

q_enact_per_term_right_normal.rationale: The LDP–Ishin government has just locked in a work-conditional credit (April 2027 start, permanent FY2029), which crowds out UBI for years. The coalition agreement omits basic income. Ishin's BI option is its only foothold, and with 316 LDP seats Ishin's leverage is small.

q_enact_per_term_left_ai_shock.rationale: A non-LDP government formed in the wake of an AI shock would likely include parties that back universal cash (Reiwa, possibly Team Mirai, which names BI for AGI scenarios). It is below the US D-trifecta (0.45) because Japanese opposition coalitions are unstable, the Finance Ministry is strongly fiscally conservative, and the mainstream centre-left designs are targeted credits.

q_enact_per_term_right_ai_shock.rationale: Higher than a US Republican analogue, because the likely coalition partner (Ishin) lists basic income as an option, Team Mirai frames BI as the AGI safety net, and the LDP delivered universal ¥100,000 cash in 2020. My Number-linked delivery built for the refundable credit could be widened. Held down by LDP work-ethic framing and the sunk investment in the work-tested credit.

q_enact_per_term_other_ai_shock.rationale: A minority or loose-support government (like LDP 2024–25) must trade policy for votes. Parties such as DPFP, Ishin and Reiwa could extract cash measures, as happened with the 'income wall' deals. Lasting universal statutes are harder than one-offs, but a shock makes them salient.

ai_shock_exposure_vs_us.rationale: Unemployment is 2.45% (World Bank 2025). A shrinking workforce means even Takaichi's government says foreign workers are still needed, and firms traditionally hoard regular workers. So AI displacement is less likely to show up as a sustained 3pp unemployment rise even if task exposure is similar to the US. Some exposure remains through white-collar and non-regular work.

ai_shock_lag_years_vs_us.rationale: Slower corporate AI adoption, lifetime-employment norms and labour shortages suggest a lag. Team Mirai's AGI 'white-collar unemployment' scenario shows the risk is recognised, but I found no evidence Japan leads.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_normal.rationale: Benchmarks against 2025 GDP per capita of about ¥5.38M (World Bank): the 2020 one-off ¥100,000 is 1.9%. Reiwa's ¥30,000/month is 6.7%. Ishin's integrated ¥60,000/month BI (replacing pension and welfare) is 13.4%. A normal-times enactment is most likely a modest universal payment.

amount_median_pct_gdppc_shock.rationale: In a shock, designs converge toward Reiwa-scale (about 6.7%) payments. Ishin's integrated ¥60–100k/month plan (13–22%) is the upper tail, capped near 15% given about 206% debt to GDP.
